thread.title: San Francisco fintech Revel opens Atlanta office

author: Mark Calvey
title: San Francisco fintech Revel opens Atlanta office
text: – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Aug 1, 2018, 2:30pm PDT Revel Systems , which provides retailers with point-of-sale systems incorporating Apple’s (NASDAQ: AAPL) iPads, has joined the stampede of Bay Area fintechs expanding into Atlanta, which some have dubbed the Silicon Valley of the South. Revel is opening an Atlanta office this month that will employ 170 people over the next few years. The Atlanta office, focused on software development and sales, is led by Revel Chief Technology Officer Erick Kobres , who previously worked at Atlanta-based NCR (NYSE: NCR). “Atlanta is a thriving financial and retail technology hub and a natural fit for global, technology-based companies,” Revel CEO Greg Dukat said in a statement. Revel, founded in 2010, will keep its headquarters at 303 Second St. in San Francisco’s SoMA neighborhood, Revel told the San Francisco Business Times Wednesday. The company employs 150 people in San Francisco and is seeking to hire another 25-plus here. Revel is just the latest Bay Area startup to find Atlanta appealing. Others expanding in the Georgia capital include Opendoor, New Relic (NYSE: NEWR), Pandora Media (NYSE: P), Instacart and Square (NYSE: SQ), which revealed today that it’s expanding its San Francisco headquarters . One Atlanta booster courting Bay Area startups and their venture capitalists for decades is tech attorney John Yates , who has been well received on recruiting trips to the Bay Area this year. “The reception during both visits was extraordinary,” Yates said. “Many of the Bay Area funds expressly mentioned that they will not invest in California, New York or Massachusetts. Instead, they’re focused on regions like the Southeast and cities like Atlanta. “Three reasons given by these funds for avoiding these traditional tech centers — valuations are overly inflated in these areas, the best tech deals are being siphoned off to a few select funds, and tech talent is just too expensive for portfolio companies to grow at the required pace,” said Yates, who is chair of the technology group at the Atlanta law firm Morris, Manning & Martin . “During my visits this year to the Bay Area, every company, fund and friend sang the same song. It’s too expensive to live in the area, buying a home is almost out of the question, and talent is difficult to find and retain.” All that makes Atlanta appealing. “Of the cities giving Silicon Valley a run for its money, Atlanta must be given serious consideration because of three things: low cost of living, great universities and a burgeoning, supportive startup community,” John Gattuso , CEO of Atlanta startup FIXD Automotive writes this month in Atlanta Inno , an affiliate of the San Francisco Business Times. He could have added to that list the city’s extensive air travel reach, thanks to Delta’s (NYSE: DAL) huge headquarters hub in Atlanta. That’s a key advantage for sales staff trying to meet with clients in the eastern half of the country and elsewhere. As for those working in Atlanta, someone earning a $95,000 salary there would have to earn $254,000 in Silicon Valley to maintain the same lifestyle, he said. “Plain and simple, a dollar spent in Atlanta goes much further than the same dollar spent in Silicon Valley. Whether it is gas, food, housing or taxes, everything is cheaper in Atlanta,” Gattuso said. – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Aug 1, 2018, 2:30pm PDT Related Content
